displayQuote: Excellence is to do a common thing in an uncommon way

meta.title: Who really said "Excellence is to do a common thing in an uncommon way"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Booker T. Washington wrote "do a common thing in an uncommon manner" in Up from Slavery (1901). The polished "Excellence is..." line is a later paraphrase.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Excellence is to do a common thing in an uncommon way'?
meta.ogDescription: Booker T. Washington really wrote "do a common thing in an uncommon manner" in Up from Slavery (1901). The "Excellence is..." wording is a paraphrase.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: 1856–1915 · American educator, orator, and founder of Tuskegee Institute
answer.sourceLine: Widely credited to Washington and genuinely rooted in his writing — he twice used the phrase “do a common thing in an uncommon manner” in Up from Slavery (1901). But the polished maxim “Excellence is to do a common thing in an uncommon way” is a later condensation, not a verbatim line, and is also loosely mis-credited to Albert Einstein.

source.heading: The real line is in Up from Slavery

docMeta.dd: “…do a common thing in an uncommon manner” (chapters XIII & XVI)
“Excellence is to do a common thing in an uncommon way” — a later paraphrase

source.excerpt: As I have said, I believe that my race will succeed in proportion as it learns to do a common thing in an uncommon manner; learns to do a thing so thoroughly that no one can improve upon what it has done; learns to make its services of indispensable value.
trail: Booker T. Washington twice wrote of doing “a common thing in an uncommon manner” in Up from Slavery (1901) — chapters XIII and XVI.
Quote sites such as Goodreads print the condensed “Excellence is…” form under Washington’s name with no source.
The same line is loosely re-credited to Albert Einstein on other quote pages, with no basis.
source.excerptNote: From chapter XVI (“Europe”). Washington uses nearly the same phrase in chapter XIII, telling of anyone who “learned to do a common thing in an uncommon manner—had solved his problem, regardless of the colour of his skin.” The condensed “Excellence is…” maxim appears in neither.

source.rightsNote: Up from Slavery was first published in 1901 and is in the public domain in the United States. The one-line “Excellence is…” maxim is a modern condensation of that public-domain text, so no separate rights attach.

author.name: Booker T. Washington
author.heading: About Booker T. Washington
author.metaLine: 1856–1915 · American educator, orator, and founder of Tuskegee Institute
author.bio: Born into slavery in Virginia, Booker T. Washington rose to lead the Tuskegee Institute and became the most prominent African American public figure of his era. His 1901 autobiography Up from Slavery preached self-reliance, practical skill, and dignity in labor — the ideas behind this quotation. His accommodationist program was famously contested by W. E. B. Du Bois.

copyAttribution: Adapted from Booker T. Washington, Up from Slavery (1901) — his words were "do a common thing in an uncommon manner."

misattribution.heading: Genuine idea, rewritten wording
misattribution.intro: The line people share is real Washington in substance — but not in wording, and not always under his name.

items.why: Washington wrote “manner,” not “way,” and never framed it as a standalone “Excellence is…” aphorism; his actual sentences in Up from Slavery are longer and about racial uplift through skill.
Some quote sites credit the line to Albert Einstein, with no documented source connecting it to him.

misattribution.truthLine: The genuine words are Washington’s, from Up from Slavery (1901): “…learns to do a common thing in an uncommon manner.”

context.heading: What Washington actually meant
lead: For Washington this was not a generic productivity slogan but a strategy for racial advancement: he argued that any person, “regardless of colour,” who learned to “do a common thing in an uncommon manner” would earn respect no community could deny. He tied it to his own experience sweeping a schoolroom at Hampton, and to a Tuskegee graduate who out-produced neighboring white farmers.
